description: We are a team of Data Science and AI students from ITSE in Santiago del Estero, Argentina. We're passionate about using NASA open data to tackle real-world problems through data analysis and machine learning. We're looking for teammates in design, web development, and communications to turn our idea into a clear, engaging prototype. All skill levels welcome!
summary: Earth by Ear turns NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into live, touchable sound. Each climate phenomenon, such as wildfires and ocean heat, has its own instrument, and its sound is computed from the values in the real EIC frames: without the data, there is no sound. Users can listen to the animations in Listen mode, or slide a finger across the map in Explore mode and hear what is happening at each place, so the data can be understood with or without sight. A listening game asks players to recognize each phenomenon and its intensity by ear, which also lets us measure whether the sound is understandable. When values rise above normal, an alert layer makes the sound tense, reflecting the urgency of climate change. It runs in any phone browser, in English and Spanish, with nothing to install. Climate data is mostly visual: Earth by Ear opens it to blind and low-vision people and to anyone who learns by listening.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth by Ear turns NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into live, touchable sound. It is designed first for museum giant screens and touch kiosks, like the video walls of NASA's EIC exhibits, and also works on any computer or phone, in English and Spanish, with nothing to install. Each phenomenon has its own tab, with the real EIC frame and its own instrument:

- Fires (NASA SVS 5113, Active Fires As Observed by VIIRS): crackling

- Ocean Heat (NASA SVS 5176, Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly): cello-like drone

- Rain & Snow (NASA SVS 4285, IMERG precipitation): drops

- Air Temperature (NASA SVS 5147, GEOS-FP near-surface temperature): warm pad and whistle

- Air Quality (NASA SVS 5151, PM2.5): muffled rumble

A welcome screen offers two modes. Standard mode shows a 3D globe (or a flat map) wrapped in the real EIC frame: drag to turn it, or use two fingers on a touch screen, and point with one finger or the mouse to hear a place. Beside the globe, big numbers show the date, the main value, its level for the period and the trend over 60 dates. Blind or low-vision mode is deliberately simple: sound and voice start on their own, spoken instructions explain the screen, sliding a finger says the continent or ocean, lifting it says the value, and "Details" reads the date, place, value with units, intensity and world average. On giant screens all controls move to the bottom, within reach of seated visitors and children, and four arrows move the cursor (tap for one step, hold to keep moving, three speeds). Kiosk mode returns to a turning-Earth welcome screen after 5 minutes, with a QR code to open the app on visitors' phones. Other tabs: an Audio Tour narrated without the screen, a listening Game, and Insights (key numbers, problems and possible solutions from our data).

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline (OpenCV, NumPy) downloads each EIC visualization from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, reads 60 frames, and converts pixel colors into values with the visualization's own colorbar (nearest color in Lab space). Fields are averaged on an area-weighted 2-degree grid; fires are detected as clusters of warm pixels. The result is packed into small JavaScript files, so the web app makes no API calls. In the browser, the Web Audio API synthesizes every sound live: higher values sound denser, brighter and louder, and west-east maps to left-right. The Web Speech API speaks in the chosen language, and the 3D globe is drawn by our own code (orthographic projection of the real frame on a canvas).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

More than 2.2 billion people live with vision impairment, and climate exhibits are almost only visual. Earth by Ear opens NASA's EIC exhibits to blind and low-vision visitors and to anyone who learns by listening, and helps any visitor take away more than a quick look at a map. It is free, open and bilingual, and it makes climate data personal: on 10-12 November 2026 the hottest place on Earth in NASA's GEOS-FP data was the Gran Chaco, next to our city.

VALIDATION

(1) The fire spots we read from the EIC frames follow NASA FIRMS VIIRS detections: rank correlation 0.67-0.94 in five regions and 0.93 over 300 region-and-window pairs in 2026. (2) Listening game with 20 people: 95% named the phenomenon by ear (chance 20%) and 85% also got its intensity right (chance 33%); one-sided binomial test p < 0.0001. (3) The loudness of the five instruments is balanced to within 4 dB. (4) Automated WCAG 2.1 A/AA accessibility audit (axe-core): 0 issues.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The sound is not a soundtrack: every note comes from values read out of NASA's own frames, so listening is another way to read the data. Visitors can touch a turning globe and hear fires crackle where they are, and a blind visitor can explore a whole museum wall with four arrows and a voice.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility first (screen readers, keyboard, large touch targets, reduced motion, no information by color alone), honesty about data limits (values come from image colors, not calibrated measurements; a 2-degree grid averages local detail; fire intensity is relative; our listening test used 20 people near the team), museum use (kiosk mode, controls within reach, balanced loudness) and zero cost (no installation, no accounts, open source).

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), Web Audio API, Web Speech API, Python, OpenCV, NumPy, pandas, axe-core, Git and GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/NicoRojasDev/earth-by-ear. Team Moroncitos: Lucas Orellana, Nicolás Rojas and Juan Sayago, data scientists (ITSE, Santiago del Estero, Argentina).
